thread.title: DLA Piper: Inside the global firm now lobbying on Duke's behalf
thread.title_full: DLA Piper: Inside the global firm now lobbying on Duke's behalf

author: Zoe Kolenovsky
title: DLA Piper: Inside the global firm now lobbying on Duke's behalf
text:
This is the last story in a three-part series about Duke’s lobbying arm. The first article broke down the numbers behind Duke’s lobbying spending, and the second explored Duke’s process for interacting with government officials.
This year, Duke is directly paying an outside firm to lobby the government on its behalf for the first time: DLA Piper. The multinational law firm has poured nearly $24.6 million into political contributions since 1990 and spent more than $2 million on lobbying since 1998, representing heavyweight clients like Goldman Sachs and Lockheed Martin.
The practice of hiring firms, though, is not unique — Duke’s peers often look outside of their campus networks for assistance in the lobbying process.
According to OpenSecrets, a research group that tracks money in U.S. politics, 1,255 lobbyists worked on education issues on behalf of 711 client organizations last year. Some of these lobbyists represent in-house staff from schools’ respective government relations offices, but many more are dedicated lobbyists working for firms hired by universities and education organizations.
To understand Duke’s relationship with DLA Piper as well as other indirect ways Duke interacts with the federal government, The Chronicle took a deeper look at what the firm is, what is in its wider portfolio and what contracting outside lobbyists looks like for other educational organizations.
Duke meets DLA
According to Chris Simmons, vice president for government relations, Duke first hired law firm DLA Piper in January 2024. The firm did not officially register with Congress to lobby for the University and health system until March and April 2025, respectively.
Simmons explained that while Duke has worked with outside firms through national associations before, DLA Piper is the first outside political consulting firm the University’s Office of Government Relations has ever directly hired.
Duke initially hired DLA Piper to navigate the outcomes of the November 2024 election, Simmons said, noting that the firm helped Duke plan for various scenarios where different political parties controlled the White House and Congress. Leading up to the One Big Beautiful Bill’s passage, the firm was focused on changing proposed tax policies and cuts to federal research funding. Since then, Duke has retained the firm for continued assistance on research funding and student financial aid programs.
“We’re going to continue to work with them into the foreseeable future,” Simmons said.
DLA Piper is a powerhouse law firm with offices in five continents and over 40 countries. Its capabilities range from advising multinational corporations on financial decisions to aiding in litigation and arbitration.
It also has a robust lobbying arm.
Among the firm’s lobbyists is former U.S. Sen. Richard Burr, a Republican from North Carolina who left Congress in 2023 and joined Duke’s Sanford School of Public Policy as a fellow the following year.
Burr was a key reason Duke chose to hire DLA Piper. According to Simmons, Duke had “a great working relationship” with Burr during his time in Congress. Simmons emphasized that Burr, who served as the ranking member on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and chaired the Senate Intelligence Committee, has a strong understanding of higher education issues, including federally funded research, student aid and universities’ international relationships.
With Burr’s support, Duke joins a trend of universities turning to lobbying voices with Republican connections in recent months.
“It’s important to work across the political spectrum,” Simmons said, echoing a point Burr made in an address on Duke’s campus last year. “North Carolina has two Republican senators, and the majority of the delegation is Republican, so it’s incredibly important to continue to strengthen those relationships.”
DLA Piper does not operate from a partisan lens; the firm’s political action committee has donated relatively evenly to Democratic and Republican campaigns over the years. With the exception of 2022, though, the GOP has gotten a slight edge since 2016.
DLA Piper primarily serves as a consultant for Duke, Simmons explained. The firm advises the University and health system on how to frame and discuss their priorities and which connections to make to further Duke’s agenda.
Though there are times when someone from DLA Piper will lobby on behalf of the University without a Duke representative present, “the vast, vast, vast majority of the time, someone from Duke is involved in that conversation,” Simmons said.
Dollars for Duke
So far this year, DLA Piper logged $200,000 in income received for lobbying on behalf of the University and health system — outside of the $597,000 registered by Duke’s own lobbyists.
This number represents “a good faith estimate of all income received from the client, other than payments unrelated to lobbying activities,” per guidance issued by the Office of the Clerk of the House of Representatives.
Duke is one of nine universities DLA Piper has contracted with since 1999, the first year the firm began filing disclosure forms with the Senate in adherence with the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995. In total, DLA Piper has lobbied on behalf of 15 clients involved in the education industry.
Two of Duke’s neighbors — the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Wake Forest University — have also retained DLA Piper. UNC-Chapel Hill hired the firm for a brief period between 2004 and 2005, then rehired them in 2024, reporting $260,000 over the five most recent quarters. Wake Forest hired DLA Piper around the same time Duke did and has reported $70,000 so far this year.
DLA Piper has also worked for a few organizations of which Duke is a member. The firm registered on behalf of the Association of American Universities in Q2 of this year, reporting $80,000 for lobbying on issues related to federal research funding. DLA Piper also works for the Atlantic Coast Conference, from which it received over $3 million for lobbying activities since 2019.
DLA Piper separates its work for the University from the work it does on behalf of the health system. Including DUHS, The firm has worked for 35 clients in the health care industry since 1999, not including organizations in the related fields of pharmaceuticals and biotechnology.
A deeper dive
The median annual income DLA Piper has reported on behalf of education-related clients is $63,750. For athletics and health care, that number comes to $33,333 and $48,571, respectively.
But these industries represent just a small fraction of the policy areas represented by DLA Piper’s lobbying force. A Chronicle analysis of all of DLA Piper’s lobbying disclosure forms found that the firm worked for 490 clients across 27 industries since 1999.
We matched clients manually to broad industry categories that may include some overlap and are not meant to be definitive. For example, we defined “retail” as companies that focus on the sale and distribution of consumer goods, but a company that both produces and distributes consumer goods would likely be coded as “manufacturing” instead of “retail.” We also combined categories that other analyses may report separately; for example, “energy” includes firms involved in the extraction of raw materials like coal and petroleum, as well as electrical utilities and clean energy developers.
Over the years, DLA Piper received the most money — over $24 million — from clients in finance, which includes everything from banks to investment managers and venture capital firms. This was followed closely by the technology and defense industries at $20.8 million and $19.6 million, respectively, then manufacturing, software, pharmaceuticals and insurance.
In terms of total spending by industries over time, health care and education came in at 19th and 21st, respectively. Education was slightly higher when spending was measured annually, placing 13th in terms of industry medians for average annual client expenditures, while health care fell to 23rd.
Many of the firm’s clients are easily recognizable. Over the years, DLA Piper has worked for such high-profile companies as Apple, Coca-Cola, Ebay, General Motors, Hyundai, OpenAI, Pfizer, the National Football League, the National Basketball Association, Rite Aid and Verizon, as well as the governments of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Several of these clients are also top employers for Duke alumni, including Microsoft, Amazon, Lockheed Martin, Booz-Allen Hamilton, Oracle and Goldman Sachs.
Neither industry was represented in the top 24 clients who have spent the most on DLA Piper lobbying over time.
Most clients have had relatively short relationships with DLA Piper. The median for clients in the education industry was just one year, though the maximum reached nine years. Only a few clients retained DLA Piper for over two decades — the PGA Tour, RTX Corporation and Independent Fuel Terminal Operators Association are tied for the longest relationship at 23 years each.
Other paths
Before Duke worked with DLA Piper, though, all its contracted-out lobbying was done through larger educational coalitions and advocacy groups.
Per the University’s Office of Government Relations website, Duke is a member of at least six higher education associations, such as the Association for American Universities and Association of American Medical Colleges. The Chronicle also identified the American Association of Colleges and Universities and Association of American University Professors as advocacy groups of which Duke is a member or has a chapter.
So far this year, those groups that reported federal lobbying spent over $2.5 million.
The AAMC has spent the most by far, logging over $64 million since 1999. The organization also spends the most annually, at $2.4 million on average.
Other educational organizations in The Chronicle’s dataset spent between $15,000 and $394,000 on average each year. The Council on Government Relations and AAC&U have never filed lobbying disclosure reports and thus are not represented in the data.
Most of the organizations worked with several lobbying firms over the years — often multiple in the same quarter. The American Council on Education hired the most, at 18, while the American Association for the Advancement of Science and AAUP each hired only one firm each.
